title: After the Permanent Plan: Post-Permanency Reviews
before: After a permanent plan is chosen, the court holds a review every six months for as long as the case stays open.
after: After a permanent plan is chosen, the child's case is reviewed at least every six months while the case stays open. Most reviews are in court. Some can be done by a county review panel, but the judge must do a review at least once a year. You can ask for the judge to do it.

title: After the Permanent Plan: Post-Permanency Reviews
before: After the long-term plan is picked, the judge checks in every six months until the case closes.
after: After the long-term plan is picked, the case is checked at least every six months until it closes. The judge must check at least once a year.

title: Appeals and Writs: Challenging a Decision
before: If you cannot afford a lawyer for the appeal, one is appointed for you at no cost.
after: If you cannot afford a lawyer for the appeal, you can ask the appeals court to give you one. Ask your trial lawyer how to do this.

title: Child Support During a Dependency Case
before: Your dependency lawyer may not handle child support, so ask who can help you.
after: Ask your lawyer for help with child support papers. Your lawyer can also help you ask to stop payments.
note: Fix's Self-Help Center sentence is already a bullet on the page, so used the record's source_says (lawyer can help stop payments) instead of repeating it.

title: Fee Waiver (FW-001): How to Waive Court Filing Fees
before: How to get your court filing fees waived if you cannot afford them
after: Juvenile dependency court does not charge a fee to file a petition. You may need a fee waiver in other courts, like family court or a guardianship case. This page tells you how to ask.

after: A fee waiver covers filing fees and the sheriff's fee to serve your papers. It does not cover everything

title: For Relatives and Close Family Friends
before: If the child does not live with you, you can still ask for visits. The judge has to consider them if they are good for the child.
after: If the child does not live with you, you can still ask for visits. The judge must think about visits for grandparents when they are good for the child. Other relatives can ask too. The judge does not have to say yes.
note: Kept the page's lead-in 'If the child does not live with you'.

title: Rehearing: When a Referee Decides Your Case
before: If a referee decided something in your case, you can ask a judge to hear it again.
after: If a referee decided something in your case, you can ask a judge to hear it again. This does not work if the referee was acting as a temporary judge. Ask your lawyer which one heard your case.

title: Rehearing: When a Referee Decides Your Case
before: If a referee decided, you can ask a judge to hear it again. You have 10 days.
after: If a referee decided your case and was not acting as a temporary judge, you can ask a judge to hear it again. You have 10 days after you get the written order.

title: Parental Rights in Dependency Court
before: Unless there are aggravated circumstances, you are entitled to services to help you reunify with your child.
after: If your child is removed, the judge must order services to help you get your child back in most cases. The law lists 17 serious situations where the judge can say no to services. If you are a father the court has not yet named a presumed parent, the judge may order services but does not have to.

title: Parental Rights in Dependency Court
before: Visits may be supervised initially but should progress as you make progress on your case plan.
after: Visits may be supervised. The judge decides. As things get better, you or your lawyer can ask the judge to change supervised visits to unsupervised visits.

title: Parental Rights in Dependency Court
before: You have the right to appeal court decisions you disagree with.
after: You can appeal most court decisions you disagree with. One big one is different: the order that sets a 366.26 hearing. To fight that order you must file a writ notice fast, usually within 7 days. Ask your lawyer the same day.

title: Parental Rights in Dependency Court
before: If you cannot afford one, an attorney will be appointed for you.
after: If you cannot pay for an attorney and your child has been removed, or the county wants to remove your child, the judge must give you one. If your child is still at home, the judge may give you one. Ask the judge at your first hearing.
note: Used 'attorney' in place of the fix's 'lawyer' to match the heading and text around it.

after: . If you say no to services, the judge must first tell you what could happen. That can include losing your parental rights and your child being adopted. You must have a lawyer and sign a form.

after: The court and the county should treat you fairly. Court rules name race, ethnicity, where your family is from, disability, sex, sexual orientation and gender identity. If you need an interpreter, ask the judge for one.
